utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case Number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we are continuing with examination-in-chief by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Weiner: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good afternoon, sir, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, yesterday we were discussing the seizure of vehicles from Croatian and Muslim citizens in Bosanski Samac. Do you know a man by the name of Aladin Jakupovic, nicknamed Dadi?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where he lived?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He lived not far from my mother-in-law, near the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he own some sort of vehicle?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He owned a BMW motorcycle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did something happen to that motorcycle?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took it away from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present when this incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife and I were on our way to my mother-in-law to bring her some things. And when we got to the intersection of Pere Bosica Street, we saw four soldiers taking this man to his house. They made him open the door of the garage and drive out his BMW motorcycle. He was resisting. Then a struggle ensued. They started beating him, threw him to the ground, started beating him. But he was a strong young man, and he was resisting, fighting back. And then from the direction of the SUP building, another four men came as reinforcement to the previous four, and they were beating him while he was on the ground, beating him with anything they could, kicked him, beat him with rifle butts, fists, anything. My wife and I left this area. But later, we heard that they had killed him. We heard many versions about his death, one of them being that after this beating, he had bled to death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, whatever happened to his bicycle or his motorcycle, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the men took the motorcycle and drove it away, just as they had pulled him or his body away, they took the motorcycle, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever see Dadi, that man nicknamed Dadi again after this incident?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you heard that he was killed, did anyone that you know ever see him again?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that incident, would you have protested any request or order that you were given?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us continue on talking about the living conditions in Bosanski Samac after the takeover -- I'll say after the conflict. Now, was there a mosque in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the mosque located, sir? Tell the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mosque was across the street from the department store, and on the other side was a park. On one side of the mosque was Pere Bosica Street, and on the other side, there was a promenade in front of the mosque, a closed-off area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just very briefly describe what the mosque looked like, whether it was new, old, large, small? Just tell the Chamber a bit what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mosque was a large one, rectangular in shape, built like a square. In front of the mosque, there was a gate; and inside of the gate, behind the gate, there were arches. It had a courtyard laid out in concrete up to the gate. It had a hedge around it and concrete columns which were linked with large pipes. There was a large plain tree on the left-hand side of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was this an old building or a newer building, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an old one, but it was very well preserved and very beautiful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did something happen to this mosque during the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was destroyed, razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened? Tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one night we heard a large explosion. I thought a grenade had hit my house. We all jumped up. One of my children had already been exchanged. The other one had escaped, so my wife and I were alone. I looked outside, and I saw there was no tile on the roof. I looked in the direction of the mosque. A lot of dust has risen and clouds of smoke were rising from the mosque, and I told my wife they had blown up the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the next day or later that morning, did you go out and see what had occurred?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell us what you saw.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got out, as many other local people from Samac did. We went to see what had happened to the mosque. There was just a lot of rubble instead of the building. In a circle of 300 to 400 metres, one of the beams of the mosque had hit Fitozovic's house. The tiles on the roofs of the surrounding houses had cracked and fell to the ground, but there was no trace of the mosque. A lot of people, a large crowd, gathered. A lot of us were Muslims, and we were very hard hit by this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what happened to the debris that was strewn all over the area?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of it was taken away, cleared, and the site remained clean as if no building had ever stood there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did the clearing work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't work there, but a lot of other people who had work duty were involved in the clearing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the people who had work duty like you had to do the clearing of all the rubble?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were you doing while the rubble was being cleared?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I mended my own roof with the help of my neighbours. My neighbours also had work duty, just as I did. And we went from house to house. We went to Samat and Rasad's house first. Then to the house of our neighbour Mirko. Then we roofed Fadil's house. Then we helped Azim and Esef [phoen] Fitozovic. Then we pulled out a large beam from one man's shop, so I spent a few days, a couple of days, mending roofs. To clear the fallen tiles and the rest of the debris.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many homes did you repair, you and the others?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we count all the houses that we worked on while we were on work duty, it was altogether 40 houses. Some of them were more damaged, some of them to a lesser extent, but it was about 40.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let me get this straight. They split up the compulsory work unit. Some of the people were involved in clearing debris and some of them were involved in repairing homes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P14A, photographs 18 and 19, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you look at those two photographs, please. Could you tell us what those are.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I speak? This is the fountain and the department store, and right here was the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you place that photo on the machine to your right and point it out to the Court, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 9 is the department store. This is the fountain, the artesian well, we called it. And here the mosque used to stand, right here in this site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you also show us on the other photograph, please. And what number is that? 18.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Department store, well, and here was the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, when you went out to see the destruction of the mosque that morning, did you see any police officers present?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any police officers come to speak to you or your neighbours concerning damage to your homes?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone investigating through the rubble looking for certain types of explosives or whatever was left of explosives?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one did. Not as long as I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, was anyone ever arrested for the destruction of that mosque?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, was there a Catholic church in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that located?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in Edvarda Kardelja Street, right across the street from the orthodox church. They were facing each other, the two churches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you please just very briefly describe what the Catholic church looked like.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Catholic church was very beautiful. It was one of the older edifices in town. It was facing Edvarda Kardelja Street. It had a bell tower, a large entrance, and it was very -- its side was very long, it was very deep.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, do we need these details? Is it not sufficient to simply say there was a Catholic church at such and such a place, and then you move on what happened to it? Do we need these details? I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I just offered to bring the details because there is no photograph of the Catholic church. We have no idea what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It does not matter. What is important is the identification of the church as a Catholic church and the venue, the place where it was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in early 1993, did something happen to that Catholic church?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us how it was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that from numerous stories I heard from my friends, namely, Mehmed Vukovic, they took it apart piece by piece. They didn't blow it up in order not to damage the Serbian church which was very close by. They used demolition balls and other machinery to demolish it. That's what my friend Mese Vukovic told me. And when they took it apart piece by piece, it was hauled away. I was never told where. In any case, it does not exist any more. It was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did the persons who worked compulsory labour, were they involved in the dismantling of the Catholic church in early 1993?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they helped to load the construction material, the pieces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the persons who were involved in this dismantling tell you what they had done?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They used shovels and spades to load it on to trucks. Those who were not mobilised into the army. They were few of such men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us continue in to the year 1992 and to the spring of summer. Are you familiar with the primary and secondary schools in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see them from my balcony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were the primary and secondary schools used in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the building of the secondary school, Catholics and a couple of Muslims were detained. In the gym of the primary school, a number of Muslims were detained, but only for a short while before they were moved to a different place. So these places were used as camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you -- you said you could see the school from your home. What could you see happening at the secondary or high school during the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One day, I saw that two men had been taken out near the gym, and they were beaten. My wife and I watched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were they beaten with?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were beaten with hands, kicked. They were also beaten with weapons. I didn't know any of the men who did the beating. I couldn't recognise them at that distance. But I could see them being taken out. It was near the gym next to the trees that were planted recently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how far were these schools from your home, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was up to 75 metres to the school playground, so it must have been around 100 or 125 metres to that spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, what were your nights like living approximately 100 to 125 metres from those schools? What were the nights like at your home?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the nights were very hard. A curfew had been introduced, and no one was allowed to move around. Hardly a night would pass without us hearing songs or moaning from the camps. The songs were nationalistic songs. We could also hear the sound of beating and moaning through the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how often did that happen?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not the only one who had that. All of Samac could hear it. But there were -- there was not one particular day when we heard it. There were many of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's move towards the end of the summer of 1992. And your son is living at your home. What is your son's name?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirza.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did something happen to Mirza on or about August 20th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 20th of August at 11.00 p.m., they -- somebody knocked on the door, banged on the door, and that was Cabasko, Bijelic's son, Nenad Bijelic, and two who were unknown to me bearing military insignia. They came to pick him up. What was the reason, I asked? And they said we have to take him for interrogation. Take him in for interrogation, and they did. Why have you come at night? I was told to shut up and keep quiet. My son was taken to the building of that Australian citizen where the command headquarters were. He was questioned, interrogated. He told us later that he was interrogated about some false information concerning him, and they let him go at 2.00 a.m. Do you want me to continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now -- yes, once your son -- did your son return home later that evening?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he returned at 2.00 a.m. He was told that he has no more work duty to perform, but to report at 5.00 p.m. in the Australian -- in the headquarters, the building of the Australian citizen. He went one day, the second day, and then on the 24th, Nenad Bijelic -- they let him go. And Nenad told him -- they played together football. He told him, "Mirza, no good is in store for you. Therefore, run, flee." On the 25th in the morning, my son came to me. He didn't say anything to his mother, but he said: "Father, I'm leaving. I'll cross the river, Sava River," and I told him, "Son, good luck." He went through a mine field. He swam over the river, and for a long time I didn't know anything else. Later, much later, I heard that he was in Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. This individual who told him to leave, that there was no good coming for him, was he a soldier?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And they were friends. He would also come to us, and they played softball together. They were really true friends up to the war, and I must say he also helped him in this situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the day that your son left on August 25th, was your son the only person to escape on that date, or did other people escape?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 25th and the 26th, 126 inhabitants of Samac swam across the River Sava.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a result of this large number of people escaping, did something happen thereafter?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The consequence of this escape, there was a new camp was set up for the civilians, elderly, women, children, and my father and my step-mother were taken in at that. Because also, my half-brother, he also swam across the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me just clarify this. Are you saying that the families, the families that remained in Bosanski Samac of those people who escaped, they were placed in a camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the name of the camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an open-type camp. They weren't arrest. They were placed in different homes, in Zasavica and they worked in these camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were people allowed to leave this camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did people go voluntarily to this camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said your father and step-mother were sent there because your step-brother had left?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your father, was he -- how old was he, first?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father was born in 1926, 1926.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was approximately 66 years old at the time. Was he still employed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What had he done for work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father was a retiree, and he opened for his son a cobbler's shop, a shoe shop, for shoe reparation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was for his son that he opened the shop?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what about you and your wife? Were you taken to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did something happen which prevented you being taken to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I was coming back from my work duty, from separation, and when they came to the house in front of us and when we were taking Maja Bradisici's [As interpreted] daughter and wife, people -- there was a lot of upheaval, and they fled and never came back for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say there was upheaval which led to -- was it the police or soldiers that came to take the people away?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have an objection. The witness has said that there was a heavy shelling on Bosanski Samac on that day, and that is why everybody has fled and never came back to take to Zasavica. If my learned colleague could clarify that because we heard very clearly in our language that that is what he said, and it's not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's what I was going to do because I was expecting that answer, having him explain what upheaval is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Weiner. You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, we have a translation issue. Can you tell us what happened which led to these police or soldiers to flee, the ones that were going to take your family to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came in front of the Sanic's house, and two others came. And heavy shelling began. They left the truck. They left everything and ran off. Later on, they came to take the truck, but they didn't contact us, come for us. So this was happening all in three or four days. 27th, my father was picked up on the 27th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's continue to move on to the beginning of the winter. Let's move to Christmas eve, December 24th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, 27th of which month?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: December 24th, 1992, Christmas eve. Can you tell us where you were at about 9.00 p.m., and what you were doing.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd -- 24th of December, I was on the Bosna River. On the 23rd of December, the use of messenger came, Subasic. He called me out, and I was told that I have received military summons, military notice. And then he went in my house, and he said: "After tomorrow, you will be going for an exchange. Rada, you will be going for an exchange." My wife was preparing for the exchange. Then on the 24th, I accompanied her for the exchange. She asked me, did I receive the military notice? She said, "If you did receive it, I'll stay with you." I said, "I did not." That was the last military notice, and I was told by the same messenger that I have to wear -- carry a rifle. On the 24th of December in the evening, I sat in the house. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: He said you would have to carry a rifle. Basically you would have to join which army, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the 4th Detachment. There was no other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Basically, are you talking about the army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you want to join the army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on December 24th, you said you were sitting in your house. Was there anyone from your family that was remaining there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife left at 10.00 a.m. in the morning, and she went for the exchange, and I remained alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now what did you do about 9.00? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I sat down. I took a photo of my children and this military summons, and I said "There's no other choice. I have to cross the Sava." I took an inflatable -- an inflatable mattress, put it around me, and then I went towards River Bosna. When I came to Sokolusa along River Bosna, I unwrapped this inflatable mattress. I lay on it and entered the Bosna River with it. When I found myself in the proximity of the bridge which had been demolished, that the mattress -- the air is escaping, and that what remains is very poorly inflated mattress. And it was very cold, much below zero. And then I don't know what happened later. After a certain some time -- may I continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you don't know what happened, did you lose consciousness?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't really know what happened to me later, because when I came to, I saw the banks of the river. I don't know where. I tried to stop, to stand, and I saw two cranes. I saw these two big cranes. I said we're on our side, and I said that is the port of Samac, and I was up there. And then I crawled, and I continued. I was crawling, and then I came to the embankment. I went up to see whether there was anybody, and then to go slowly back home as if nothing happened. But the moment I came to the top of the embankment, Sisic grabbed me by the hand. He lived in Srpska Varos, and he was a truck diver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you arrested at that time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He grabbed me by the hand. He didn't say anything. Then Andra came, and Andra shouted "Ha. We've caught an Ustasha." Then they informed everybody and Vlado Sisic came to apprehend me. He had them beat me with whatever they could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say they beat you with whatever they could, what did they beat you with?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hands, feet, and weapons. After that, they took me through the town, and they took me through my street. He showed me my house. He said, "Look" and I looked. And he told me, "You'll never see it again." And I answered: "I know." Then we went on. They brought me to the command, to Mustafa Smajic's house where the command was. Again, they took me upstairs in a big room with -- where Mile Pancir was, then Mladen Roda, and then a teacher, Bosko Bosic from Gradacac, and a person sitting at the desk who was writing. I don't know who the person was. And they began beating me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they beat you with?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlado Sisic had a knife in his hand, and he turned it around. Then they spat at me. They cursed my balija's mother. They called me also "Ustasha" because I was also swimming, trying to get across. Then Bosko Bosic was hitting me the most, with a butt, kicking me, with his hands. Then Mladen Roda came in. He looked at me. He said, do you know me? I said yes. And he hit me only once. He was the chief there, the commander. Then, Bosko Bosic, they took a cigarette butt, and they put out the cigarette butt on my hand -- on my skin, but they pulled me out half dead from the cold water and I didn't even feel it that much. And then Mile Pancir took me to another place. They took me to the bathroom where in the bathtub, they filled it and they placed me and they told me: "Show Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. us how you swam, how you swim on the other side." They wanted to drown me. Mile Pancir stepped -- pressed here with his knee at here, and with one hand, with one finger, he tried to get out my eyeball. And then Roda came and said "stop." He moved. Then they stripped me, and they opened in the bathroom there was a cupboard, and they gave me some clothing of the owner of the house, and then I dressed that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a few questions. You said they filled up a bathtub and tried to drown you. Did they put you in the bathtub?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they filled the bathtub to the top, Mile, Mile Pancir. He tried to make me dive, and Sisic helped him, assisted him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that Mile Pancir put his knee to your face, and you pointed to your cheekbones. Explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First he threw me on the floor, and he was pressing with his knee on my cheekbone. And he tried with his finger to get out the -- my eye. And -- but then their commander came and said "stop".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during this time, did they ask you any questions? Were you interrogated at any time during this beating?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they asked me quite banal, superficial matters. Who is the organiser of all these escapes from Samac? And what is the password which you're to say when you come to the other bank? I didn't know that, and I say that I never knew it and that nobody knows that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any document ever prepared for you to sign based on this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sign a document?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to read it before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't interested in it. I didn't look at it, and I didn't dare look at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what was in the document that you signed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after they gave you some dry clothes, what did they do with you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took me downstairs and they took me to this -- to the place in front of the building in the guards' shed, and then they placed me in a car and took me to the village of Slatina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they take you in the village of Slatina?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the Catholic Slatina. There was nobody there except for the military. They took me to a military command headquarters where I could see the insignia, the Krajina military police. They took me to a private house in this village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in the village of Slatina with the Krajina military police?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed there three days. And they were quite correct. They handcuffed me. I slept in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you beaten there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after those three days, where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, they took me to the police station, police station in Samac for interrogation. I stayed there for a short time, and then they took me to Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at the police station in Samac, were you questioned?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. The interrogation was carried out by a person I didn't know at all, and the same questions were repeated as before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you given a statement to sign? Or was a statement prepared based on your questioning?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I signed, but I didn't look at the paper, what it contained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you write the information that was on that paper that you signed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what is contained in that information that you signed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask to read it prior to signing it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you feel while you were in the police station at -- in Bosanski Samac during those few days, short time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were correct in their treatment of me. They didn't beat me. But they interrogated me. I was staying there alone. The camp didn't exist any more, and there were no other prisoners except me. I was wondering what would happen with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you eventually go to Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the police station in Bosanski Samac, they let me go home. This policeman told me, who was -- I knew him also earlier. And he told me: "You're going home." I really didn't believe it, and I didn't even move. And he said: "You're going home, go, move." Then I went towards my home. I stayed there for two days. On the third day, they told me to get ready and that I'll be going to Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you went to Pelagicevo. Where did they hold you in Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Pelagicevo, they kept me in a shop, in a department store called Trgocentar. I was never there before. But next to it is the veterinary station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did something happen to you at the end of January? On January 29th, did you receive some sort of a notification while in Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 29th of January, in Pelagicevo, they took me for a number of interrogations. Then I had work duty, and I was informed that on the 29th, the next day, I would go in for an exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you're notified that you're going to go in for an exchange? What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't believe it. And then they came for me by car, a policeman from Samac. He picked me up and took me home. He was supposed to be with me at home, but he left me alone, and he went home as we knew each other since earlier times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the next morning, on January 30th, 1993, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the next morning, I went in front of -- to the building of retirees, and the buses were already aligned there for the exchange of civilians. I entered -- mounted a bus, sat down, and waited for the bus to depart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before you got on the bus, did you see any of the defendants there at the retirement home? Did you see any of the defendants?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Tadic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he doing?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was standing there. He was the one who organised it. He wasn't reading the names out. It was Sveto Vasovic who did that. He was the organiser of the exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your name read out?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you got on the bus after it was read out?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who else was on the bus?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Children, women, all of them civilians from Bosanski Samac, old and young. If you look at us men, there were very few of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did the bus eventually leave?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bus set off in the direction of Bijeljina, and from there to Racca which is a crossing point towards Serbia

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did something happen when you got to Racca?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived at Racca, I was told to get off the bus and to get on to another bus. When I did that, I saw my fellow citizens from Samac inside that bus, plus some people who had been detained in the Batkovic camp. They were on that bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took us to Lipovac where the exchange took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you got to Lipovac, just tell the Court what happened?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since I knew from before that in all exchanges somebody always failed to be exchanged, I sat on the first seat. And when the bus stopped, I got out first and was the first in line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you exchanged sometime thereafter?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were any of the defendants present?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Tadic. He was the big boss. He was the one telling people who to release, who to let go. Tadic entered a small marquee that had been improvised on the spot. Everybody would enter, tell their name, get registered, and get out on the other side and be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did they exchange everyone together, or were there separate exchanges for civilians and soldiers? How did it work, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilians were not exchanged. A bus load of them simply got out and crossed over to the other side. However, my group was exchanged almost as prisoners of war. That's at least what it looked like. We were exchanged on a one-for-one basis. I was exchanged for a Serb man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at this time of exchange, could you describe yourself physically? Did you have any physical injuries at this time, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't looking well. I was a sorry sight indeed, having gone through all that I had been through, all the beatings, all the humiliations and degradations. I was not -- I didn't resemble a human being at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you suffer any broken bones as a result of that beating in Bosanski Samac after you attempted to escape?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a rule that everybody went first to see a doctor, so I went to see a doctor in Majavac [phoen]. I told them to look at my eyeball. They sent me for an x-ray. The bone over my eye was not broken. They told me there was no need for surgery unless I wanted plastic surgery for esthetic reasons. And I said no, I won't do that unless there are other consequences. So I didn't do anything about it, and my eye is simply somehow pushed deeper inside. That's the only thing you can notice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you feel physically at that time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Horrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you exhausted?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was exhausted, and I suffered from all kinds of pain all over my body. Everything hurt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have those same pains prior to the conflict erupting?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had back problems, but not that bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just a couple other matters relating to family property. You indicated that your father had a cobbler or a shoe repair shop in Bosanski Samac, and he had it -- put it together for one of your brothers or you said for one of his sons. What happened to that shop in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was seized as soon as he was taken to Zasavica. They also seized his apartment in town as soon as he was taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when he was taken away on August 27th, they seized both his apartment and his cobbler shop?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did someone move into those two locations?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, later, after the war ended, somebody moved immediately into the apartment. I don't know who. But after the war ended, the cobbler's shop was taken over by someone. I don't know who again. But I know the shop was open for customers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you re-obtained that shop? Has your family re-obtained that shop?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my father regained his apartment, and I didn't ask about the rest. My father died in America three or four years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your father ever give anyone permission to take his apartment or his shop?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever receive any rent for anyone using his apartment or his shop?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about any rent for anyone using his equipment in the shop?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about your home, sir. At the time of the -- of your exchange, in January 1993, who was living in your home?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was exchanged, naturally, they seized my home for their own purposes, and the apartment I owned was taken over by the man who interrogated me at the SUP. I know him. He is a Samac man, but I don't know him personally. Nobody dared approach my house and ask anything. So that man lived in it. Last year, I regained my house. I got it back, and I have some cousins in Samac whom I authorised to deal with all the legal stuff connecting -- connected with getting my house back and looking after it until I return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to the house being seized, which was after you got exchanged, prior to that, were any of your relatives living in that house?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mother and father-in-law were with me. When I was exchanged -- my father-in-law actually died in my home while I was still there. And after I was exchanged, nobody remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your wife's brother's family? Where were they living?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They spent a couple of days in my house. They thought they would stay with us. But at one point, they got so scared they went back to their own home. They thought they would be better off there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What scared them?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Day in, day out policemen would come to my house and people who were interested in my house, in getting it for themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did a policeman eventually move into that house?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that man moved in. I don't know whether he was a policeman. He was some sort of low-rated inspector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did that man live there in your house?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until last year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever give him any permission to move into your home?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever pay you any rent during those nine years?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you want that person living in your home, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you got your house back in 2001, what was the condition of the house?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the outside, it was the same as I left it. But inside, there was no trace that I had ever lived there. Nothing of my possessions remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any furniture left in the house?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the heating system?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The heating system was electrical. I also had a firewood stove, but nothing, nothing remained when I saw it again. Not even a light bulb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the little fast-food restaurant, if you want to call it, the kabob restaurant that you had out in front of your house? What happened to that building?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody, they don't know who, dismantled the windows and the door and took them away. And a different iron door was placed instead of my door, and there was nothing inside. You couldn't ever gather that it used to be a shop or anything else. Clear space.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, prior to the war, you had this property, little business, a job. Back in April of 1992, did you like living in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your family happy there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you plan to leave Bosanski Samac, this place where your family had lived for generations, back in April of 1992 prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You enjoyed living there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after the war starts, sir, was your family safe in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were. You mean after the beginning, or before the war?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, after the war. Was your family safe?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the war started, were you and your family safe in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you subjected to certain restrictions on your freedoms after the war started?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you treated differently from the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you still able to make choices relating to your family, whatever choices you wanted, after that war started?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if not for these change in conditions and the compulsory labour, would you have wanted to leave Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the members of your family, would they have wanted to leave if not for these change in conditions and the compulsory labour?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object to the phrasing of the Prosecutor's question. He has asked two questions using the term "forced labour." I think we can talk about work duty as my colleague Mr. Pantelic has already pointed out, not forced labour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I used "compulsory labour" on both occasions. The witness and the other witnesses have testified continually that they did not volunteer to do any of this labour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, it's all right to use compulsory labour. I think maybe it's the interpretation which is not reflecting compulsory labour but may be reflecting "forced labour." I'd like to know from the interpreters, whether that is the same, compulsory labour and forced labour, is that the same term in Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe I can be of some assistance, Your Honour. My colleagues just here told me that they received the term "forced labour" in B/C/S language. Obviously compulsory labour is something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's why I asked the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My suggestion to interpreters would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, I didn't ask you to instruct the interpreters. You are not here to instruct them. They know what to do. I just wanted to ask whether the terms are different.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is possible to make the distinction. We will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: They can make a distinction in the interpretation. So Mr. Weiner, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's it. No further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Cross-examination. Who is going to start? Or there's no cross-examination? Hopefully. Yes, Mr. Pisarevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Pisarevic:

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I apologise for this shuffling. I will now start my questioning of Mr. Nusret Hadzijusufovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Mr. Nusret, I am Borislav Pisarevic, and I represent Mr. Simo Zaric here. I will be asking you questions pertaining to certain facts, and I would appreciate it very much if you could answer to my questions with "yes," "no," or "I don't know," if that is the case, all with a view to completing this cross-examination as efficiently and as soon as possible. Before I ask my first question, I wish to express to you on behalf of my client, Mr. Simo Zaric, his heartfelt regret of everything that you and your family have gone through and suffered during this unfortunate conflict in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the town of Samac itself where you resided. The first question I want to ask you is this: Are you aware of the fact that the 4th Detachment of the Yugoslav People's Army, which was part of the 17th tactical group, was established on the 5th of January, 1992? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that on the 13th December, 1991, on the territory of the former Socialist Federation Republic of Yugoslavia, the Presidency proclaimed general mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of 1991 and 1992, were you a military conscript?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a citizen, were you assigned to any other unit or formation or any other defence structure in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you assigned to the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you relieved of military duty?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an assignment to the civilian defence?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an obligation to work in your company?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in the event of any immediate danger of war or war itself, you, as a citizen of the federal republic of Yugoslavia had absolutely no obligations or duties?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I just want to object at this time. This is part of our continuing objection. He is asking questions concerning the term "obligation." At that point, there was a new government. It was the BiH government. He had no obligations. This strictly concerns assignments under the former government. And I think his question should reflect that. The term "obligation" is different because obligation you have to believe that there is still a government existing and that you would be obligated to serve. That government had split up. There was now a republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which had been recognised. So the term "obligation" in incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought that that is the other matter which has to be decided after the trial as to what was the legitimate government, what was the status of that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Correct. However, the wording should be "assignment." "Were you assigned by the former government?" And under our previous objections the Court has usually required them to indicate under the former government, that you had former assignments, or you were assigned by reason of the former government's authorisation. You are asking current obligations. How can this man determine if he had an obligation. That is a decision that this Court or lawyers is going to have to determine concerning what was a legitimate and illegitimate government and he can't make a legal determination whether or not he has obligations -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think it's a question language. If the witness is asked, "Did anybody tell you to work in here during a particular period?" perhaps that would be much easier. It would be neutral and then the witness won't know whether anybody did assign him anything at any particular period during the material period that the indictment is covering. I think it's a question of the term that you are using, if you can make it a neutral term.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I am questioning this witness precisely to the period of 1991 and to the period until the 17th of April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this period, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia still existed, the Yugoslav People's Army was still in existence. And as far as the legality of the existence and presence of the JNA in the territory of BH, it is a different issue, a legal issue. I cannot ask this witness questions that would put him in an impossible position. I cannot now enter into a debate with the Prosecutor as to what was legal and illegal and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: As long as you have specified which period. You have explained that your questions are pertaining to the period of 1991 up to 17th April, though the transcript shows 1994, I'm sure you meant 1992. So if you specify the period, and then you put the questions to the witness. I'm sure you understand the objection by Mr. Weiner is the fact that this witness is a fact witness, and he can only deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just one other thing, Your Honour. Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised on the 6th of March, 1992. And Judicial notice has been taken by this Chamber of that. However, the April 17th is the date of the conflict, so there's -- any time you even get near that question, there seems to be problems that arise. It would have to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right, yes. It may be that fact of the date of the 6th of March can be taken into account by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it's a mistake of my learned friend Mr. Weiner. It is actually 6th of April. It's not a recognition. In general terms, it is only recognition of European Union and United States of America which at that time was only 13 members of the world community. That's the fact. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, you should wait until the Trial Chamber gives you permission to speak. Because your colleague is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. That's my mistake. I do apologise again. I'm very sorry. Terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wanted to indicate to my learned colleague, Mr. Weiner, it's a question of the approach. We know that Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised by certain countries on the 6th of April; however, our stand is that Bosnia-Herzegovina became the legal subject, international legal subject, on the 22nd of May, when it became a full member of the UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, can we stop that debate. Can we just go back to cross-examination and see how the cross-examination goes. We are ready to take our break, and we will continue the proceedings at 16.15 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, cross-examination continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Mr. Hadzijusufovic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to Their Honours, when did you -- were you free of any obligations towards the military?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1988, and Dr. Stanko was a member of the committee when that occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Secretariat of the Defence gave you the document on the relief of this obligation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, in the period from the 1st of January, 1992, until the 17th of April, 1992, did you know of the existence of the 4th Detachment of the JNA in Samac, the 1st of January, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that you absolutely did not know about the existence of the 4th Detachment in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- I have heard that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we agree that you had some knowledge that you've heard that in the city of Samac, there was the 4th Detachment in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the fact? Are you aware of the fact that the command of the 4th Detachment was in the building, the SIT headquarters, in the period February, March, to the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you move -- pass by that building on your way to work and when returning from work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this building, the SIT, the building called Mladost, did you see the banner of the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia and of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know or did you hear that the commander of the 4th Detachment was Radovan Antic who was a reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that the deputy commander of the 4th Detachment of the JNA was Jovo Savic, the reserve captain also from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that Simo Zaric is a reserve sergeant, and that he was also responsible for information and questions of the morale issues?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that the operations officer in the command of the 4th Detachment of the JNA was the reserve officer Mehmed Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm that you know Mr. Mehmed Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that same person, Mehmed Vukovic, who spoke to you about the demolishing of the Catholic church?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mehmed Vukovic ever speak about the fact that he had been a member and an operations officer in the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see the list of members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the members of the 4th Detachment walk around town in the JNA uniforms?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is saying depending on which period.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are still in the period of prior to the 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please a more close date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the 5th of January, to the 17th of April, 1992, did you ever see members of the 4th Detachment walking in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them a few days before the outbreak of war. And more when I saw Tota and Danilo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see them walking in the town along the street?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them walking by my street. I didn't see them in town itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they carry also weapons?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did, these three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see the soldiers of the 4th Detachment lined up?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them on Sokolusa, not in military uniform. That is the next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the number of members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your statement, you stated that the civilians you've seen attending military exercise, you identified them as members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you answer the question: In what way, how did you identify them as such?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I saw them during the war in uniform, these very same people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we agree, then, that when you saw them then, at that military exercise, at that time, you didn't know that they were members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From talking to others, I knew it. However, I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It implies that you personally did not see and personally weren't convinced they were members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was convinced of it during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were watching this military exercise, by no sign or insignia, you couldn't determine that these were members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had no insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we then agree that your knowledge concerning the 4th Detachment of the JNA are mainly based on hearsay, based on sources which aren't reliable and are not sure?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. What are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He is saying number one, the information that you have is mainly based on hearsay. Hearsay is a legal term. If it is an admission from a member of the 4th Detachment which he has testified to, then it's not hearsay because it's an admission against interest technically. So legally it is not hearsay. I think he should use another term if he wants to say that he received it from what type of sources or other sources, but the use of hearsay I don't think is a valid question, because you're asking him to make a legal decision as to whether or not something is hearsay. If you consider the 4th Detachment an illegal operation or just as a group itself, the fact that one person in that group admits to being part of that group or tells him he's part of that group, that would fall under the exception to the hearsay rule of being an admission basically, similar to a party opponent, or I would at least argue that it's similar to a party opponent, so hearsay isn't the proper term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are not receiving translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we find out why there's no interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at a certain point, I didn't have the translation. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Now you have it. Can you hear?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I hear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe Mr. Weiner can repeat his grounds for objection. Slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sorry, Your Honour. He asked the question of whether or not the information that he received is based on hearsay, and then he also questioned the reliability of sources. Number one, I would say that's a multiple issue question. Is it based on hearsay? Is it based on unreliable sources? But first let's start off with the hearsay. Hearsay is a legal phrase, whether or not something is hearsay is a legal decision. The fact that someone says something to another person doesn't automatically make it hearsay, even if it's said outside of the context here. It is -- it could fall under an exception to the hearsay rule, and then not technically be hearsay, or if you want to call it admissible hearsay at the least. So whether or not something is hearsay I don't think is the proper question to ask this witness. Number two, he also asked a multiple question which is in addition to whether or not it's hearsay, whether or not it's from unreliable sources. That's a multiple question. If he says yes, is he saying yes to it's hearsay or is he saying yes to its unreliable sources. He should ask separate questions; if he got from other persons and then if he got it from unreliable sources. And my question relating to hearsay was -- my issue linked to hearsay was the fact that someone who is a member of that organisation provides information to him, that that person is a member of the organisation, that other persons are members of the organisation, would that become an admission? And if it is an admission, whether it's a declaration against interest or it's just an admission, whether a party opponent or just an admission period, does that take it outside the realm of hearsay. Therefore, I think it's an improper question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, counsel. I was waiting for --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What you can do is rephrase your question, and make sure it's only one question at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzijusufovic, would you please answer, in what way did you find out who the members of the 4th Detachment are?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them in war, and through talks with individual members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you quote names of certain people that you had seen at the exercise in Sokolusa for whom you assert that they are members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of those that I have spoken of, all of those who questioned me and who were beating me at that time. The names, Antic, Tota, Nikica, Nenad Bijelic, he son of Smotar [As interpreted]. No other names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody ask you to join the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody force you to join -- did anybody coerce you? The fact that you did not join the 4th Detachment, that is a reflection of your free will.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a reflection of my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your personal opinion --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The answer to the first question on page 40, line 19, is not in the transcript, and the witness answered "no." The question was: "Did anybody force you to join -- did anybody coerce you to join the 4th Detachment?" The witness said "no." And the answer is not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps Mr. Pisarevic can refer that back to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzijusufovic, did anybody coerce you to join the 4th Detachment of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the counsel here, the Trial Chamber, when you were watching them, what were they doing there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply training, physical training preparation, running. Simply running.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they do anything else?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this running, here in front of the Trial Chamber, you described it as "military exercise." Is that it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you've mentioned your neighbour, Mr. Slobodan Kukrika. You said that he had a submachine-gun 84.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, we are not particularly pleased with the translation. It is not submachine-gun. Actually, it is a machine-gun, a large one. It is not a small size machine-gun. It is a huge machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What you're saying is it shouldn't be translated as submachine-gun. It is just a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters disagree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
